lesson.title: Implicit Equations: Curves That Refuse to Be a Single Formula
lesson.summary: An implicit equation relates x and y directly, often tracing curves such as circles or the folium of Descartes that no single explicit formula y = f(x) can describe in full, which is exactly the setting where implicit differentiation becomes necessary rather than optional.
lesson.body:
An implicit equation is any equation relating x and y where neither variable has been solved for in terms of the other, such as x^2+y^2=25, x^3+y^3=6xy, or y^5+xy=3. These equations describe curves in the xy-plane, but unlike y=f(x), a single implicit equation can trace out a shape that is not the graph of one function at all, since a vertical line can cross the curve more than once, violating the vertical line test that defines a function in the first place.

The circle x^2+y^2=25 makes this concrete: a vertical line at x=3 crosses the circle at both (3,4) and (3,-4), so the full circle is not a function of x. Yet locally, near the point (3,4) alone, the upper arc of the circle does behave like a function, since a small enough vertical strip around x=3 only intersects that one arc once. This local, piece by piece view of an implicit equation, function like near most individual points even when the whole curve is not a function, is what justifies applying derivative techniques to implicit equations at all, and it is the same local reasoning introduced with implicit functions in the previous topic.

Take the implicit equation x^2+y^2=25 again and differentiate both sides with respect to x, treating y as an implicit function of x. The left side term x^2 differentiates to 2x as usual. The term y^2 requires the chain rule, since y is not the independent variable but a function of x: using the power chain rule with u=y, d/dx[y^2] = 2y times dy/dx. The right side, the constant 25, differentiates to 0. So 2x + 2y(dy/dx) = 0, giving dy/dx = -x/y. At the point (3,4), dy/dx = -3/4, matching the result found earlier by solving explicitly for y = sqrt(25-x^2) and using the general power rule, where the derivative was also computed as -3/4, so both approaches, implicit and explicit, agree perfectly at this point.

This differentiate both sides technique, called implicit differentiation, depends entirely on the chain rule machinery built throughout this chapter: every term involving y needs an extra factor of dy/dx tacked on, precisely because y is being treated as an unnamed but differentiable function of x, the same idea introduced with implicit functions. Without the Leibniz chain rule and the power chain rule already in hand, the step from y^2 to 2y(dy/dx) would have no justification, and the entire technique would be little more than an unexplained trick rather than a direct application of rules already proven.

Implicit equations matter beyond circles: they describe ellipses, hyperbolas, and far more exotic curves like the folium of Descartes, x^3+y^3=6xy, none of which can be written as one tidy explicit formula for y. Implicit differentiation, previewed here through the circle example, is the general method that makes slopes and tangent lines available on all of these curves without ever needing to solve for y first, and it is the natural next technique to develop now that implicit functions and implicit equations are both established as ideas.
